title: Viewing the NFT on the Frontend
section: 42. Minting NFTs and Building an NFT Marketplace like OpenSea
summary: Renders the minted NFT in the React Item component: pass the canister id as a prop, create an HttpAgent and an actor from the generated idlFactory, load name, owner and image bytes on mount with useEffect, and turn the byte array into a Blob object URL for the img tag. The owner field is a learner challenge.

concepts.heading: Starting the frontend
points: Run npm start and open localhost:8080: header, footer and the static home image appear; nothing is clickable yet.
In App.jsx, comment out the home image (and its import) and render the Item component instead. Letting the editor autocomplete the component name inserts the import automatically, avoiding typos.
Item.jsx is plain markup: a card with an img, the name heading and an 'Owner:' line. Layout/centering is fixed in later lessons. Initially these are hardcoded values.

concepts.heading: Passing the canister id as a prop
points: Get the minted canister's id with dfx canister id nft.
In App, store it in a constant (e.g. nftId) and pass it down as a prop named id: <Item id={nftId} />. In Item read props.id.
This id is later used to address the right canister, so each Item can show a different NFT.

concepts.heading: HttpAgent: talking to the canister over HTTP
points: Calling a canister from the browser means HTTP requests to the replica. Locally that is the local dfx address; define it as a localHost URL string.
HttpAgent comes from @dfinity/agent: import { HttpAgent } from "@dfinity/agent" (case-sensitive; watch the spelling of dfinity).
const agent = new HttpAgent({ host: localHost }); the constructor takes an options object where host is the replica URL.
(Extra) In the reference repo the host constant is a localhost port; use whichever address your dfx or proxy actually serves.

concepts.heading: Actor.createActor and the idlFactory
points: Calls are asynchronous, so they happen in an async function, here loadNFT().
Create the actor: await Actor.createActor(idlFactory, { agent, canisterId }). First argument: the interface factory; second: options, including the agent and the target canister id.

idlFactory is exported from the generated declarations folder, in nft.did.js. It describes the Motoko canister's interface (methods getAsset, getName, getOwner, their inputs and outputs) in JavaScript terms, acting as a translator between frontend and Motoko.
Import path from the component: three levels up, then declarations/nft, i.e. ../../../declarations/nft. Note exact casing: idlFactory.
canisterId must be a Principal object, not a string. Import Principal from @dfinity/principal and wrap props.id with Principal.fromText(props.id).

concepts.heading: When to load: useEffect with an empty dependency array
points: The NFT should be fetched once, on the first render. Use useEffect(() => { loadNFT(); }, []).
The second argument is the dependency list; empty means run only after the first render, otherwise the fetch would repeat on every state update.

concepts.heading: Name, owner and image
points: Name: const name = await NFTActor.getName(); then setName(name) using a state variable created with useState() (initially undefined). Replace the hardcoded heading text with {name}. The demo shows it changing to the minted CryptoDunks name.
Owner (challenge): await NFTActor.getOwner() returns a Principal; call .toText() before storing it so React can render it, then setOwner. Replace the hardcoded owner text with {owner}.
Image: getAsset() returns an array of 8-bit numbers. Wrap it in new Uint8Array(imageData) so JavaScript treats it as bytes.

Create a Blob from it: new Blob([imageContent.buffer], { type: "image/png" }). A Blob takes an array of parts and optional options such as the MIME type (see MDN). .buffer gives the underlying ArrayBuffer.
URL.createObjectURL(blob) returns a temporary URL string usable as the img src. Store in an image state variable and set src={image}.
Result: the card shows the minted name, the owner principal and the pixel-art image from the chain for the first time.

task.name: Show the owner from the NFT canister
task.starting_point: Item.jsx already loads and displays the NFT name from getName() via state, but the owner line is still hardcoded.
task.goal: Replace the hardcoded owner with the real owner principal of the minted NFT, displayed as text.
steps: Add const [owner, setOwner] = useState(); in Item.
Inside loadNFT call const owner = await NFTActor.getOwner();.
Convert the Principal with owner.toText() and pass the result to setOwner.
Replace the hardcoded owner in the JSX with {owner}.
Save, refresh and compare with the output of dfx canister call nft getOwner.
task.expected_result: A long principal id equal to the one used when minting appears after 'Owner:'.
task.reference_repo_path: Section 42 - Minting NFTs and Building an NFT Marketplace like OpenSea/42.03 Viewing the NFT on the Frontend/OPEND/src/OPEND_frontend/src/components/Item.jsx

pitfalls: Typos in HttpAgent, @dfinity/agent, or idlFactory casing.
Passing a string where a Principal is needed (forget Principal.fromText).
Forgetting await on actor creation or on the method calls.
Putting a Principal object in JSX instead of toText().
Omitting the empty array in useEffect, causing repeated fetches.
Using the wrong dfx address as host.
(Extra) The reference repo has typos (imageContant) and a hardcoded canister id and port; replace them with your own. Its Item.jsx builds the agent on each render, which is fine for the demo.

gaps_and_ideas: Proposed lesson 'Turning bytes into an image': blurb on getting binary data from a backend and showing it in the browser.

Tasks: 1) make a Uint8Array from an array of numbers; 2) wrap it in a Blob with type image/png; 3) create an object URL and assign it to an img; 4) load the data once with useEffect and []; 5) convert a mock Principal to text before rendering.
Starter code: a fake async NFT actor returning getName/getOwner/getAsset with a tiny PNG byte array.
Explore demo idea: an editable byte array with a live image preview, plus a toggle showing what happens with the wrong MIME type or without revoking the object URL.
